archetype.name: Game Manager (spot starter)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup asked to run a run-first offense behind an elite defense: he throws on time, mostly short, feeds his best receiver and avoids the mistakes that defined his early career.

report.headline: A career-best efficiency spike built on short throws, Smith-Njigba and a great defense
report.take:
Drew Lock is filling in for Sam Darnold again, and on a three-game sample he has been one of the most efficient passers in the league. His 0.355 EPA per dropback ranks 2nd of 49 qualifiers, and he has no interceptions, no lost fumbles and a 2.6% sack rate that ranks first. Nothing in his career looks like this. His 2020 season as a full-time starter came with 15 interceptions and a -5.5 CPOE, and his 2024 Giants stint graded at -0.136 EPA per play, 49th of 60. So the first question is not whether he has changed. It is what in his situation is producing these numbers.

The answer is mostly structure. Seattle passes 5.9 points less often than situation predicts (27th), sits behind the 5th-ranked defense, and has played three low-scoring games that all went under. Lock's intended air yards are 6.84 and his throws land about two yards short of the sticks on average. His time to throw, 2.64 seconds, is quicker than anything he posted in Denver or New York. He is pressured on only 11.5% of dropbacks (3rd lowest) and has a 7.9% bad-throw rate (2nd best). This is a quarterback being kept clean and kept simple. The closest match in his history is his 2019 rookie cameo, when a 6.9 aDOT produced a respectable 0.104 EPA per play.

The numbers also hide how concentrated the production is. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has drawn 31 targets at 0.74 EPA per target, worth 23 EPA of the 32 Lock has generated on all dropbacks. Nobody else comes close, and Rashid Shaheed has been a net negative. The deep line of 1.971 EPA per attempt rests on five throws. The 14 screens and swings behind the line have cost him EPA despite a 100% completion rate. The efficiency is real in the sense that he isn't giving the ball away. The scale of it comes from one receiver and a handful of explosive throws.

Where this heads depends on the line in front of him. Quenton Nelson (knee procedure) and Charles Cross (ankle) are both out. They are 99% and 98% snap starters on a team whose offense already ranks 28th in hit rate allowed. Lock's clean-pocket profile is the foundation of everything above. Losing two starters up front is the most direct threat to it, more than any regression in touchdown rate.

strengths.title: Turnover-free, on-time decision making
strengths.body: Zero interceptions, the league's lowest sack rate and the second-best bad-throw rate add up to a quarterback who isn't hurting his team. The cause is a quicker, shorter process than he ever ran in Denver, inside an offense that asks little of him. The zero will not last, given his career. But the habit of getting the ball out has held across all three games.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba pays off
strengths.body: Lock has locked onto his best receiver, and it has worked: 31 targets at 0.74 EPA per target, carrying most of his passing value. Leaning on a separator is good quarterbacking in a backup role, not a flaw. As long as Smith-Njigba is healthy, this floor stays.

strengths.title: Sharp off play-action looks
strengths.body: Under center he has posted 0.475 EPA per play with a 64% success rate and 79.2% completions, well above his shotgun work. That fits a run-heavy offense that sells the run and gives him defined throws. On 25 plays it is a hint, not a fact, but it matches how Seattle uses him.

concerns.title: Two starting linemen out
concerns.body: Nelson and Cross are both out, and Seattle already ranks 28th in hit rate allowed. Lock's low pressure rate is the backbone of his efficiency. His career pressure-to-sack numbers in 2021, 2023 and 2024 show what happens when the pocket collapses on him. This is the concern most likely to show up immediately.

concerns.title: Career says this regresses
concerns.body: Every prior season sits at or below average in EPA and CPOE, with 2020's 15 interceptions the low point. The current line comes from three games and five deep attempts producing outsized value. Expect the interception-free run and the deep efficiency to come back toward his norms, even if the short game holds.

concerns.title: Oblique strain and a quieter last game
concerns.body: He was limited in practice with an oblique strain, though his coach expects him to manage it. Week 9 was his least efficient game: -2.9 CPOE and 5.4 intended air yards against a weak Arizona defense. An oblique can sap torque on throws, so watch whether the ball keeps getting shorter.

trend.note: Two solid, modest games (6.4 and 5.1 passing EPA) sandwich one big outing against Arizona in Week 2 (16.1). The baseline is efficient and low-volume, and the most recent game was the most conservative of the three.

nextGame.headline: Raiders' leaky short-pass defense suits him, if the patched line holds
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas matches Lock's profile about as well as any defense could. It ranks 28th in pass EPA allowed and 31st in success rate, and it is dead last against short passes, which is exactly where Lock lives. Quarterbacks have scored the most touchdowns per game against the Raiders in the league and the third-most PPR points. The game is indoors, Seattle is a 3.5-point favorite, and the 43.5 total is higher than any of Lock's three games so far. That leaves some room for a more open script than the grind-it-out wins he has been part of.

Availability cuts both ways. Lock himself is questionable with the oblique but trending toward playing, and Darnold's expected return is not until late November. Seattle is missing Cross and Nelson up front, and the Raiders rank 8th in hit rate, so the replacements will be tested. Shaheed is out too, but his targets have been unproductive, so his absence matters less than it sounds. On the Raiders' side, the only relevant defensive absence is a rotational tackle, Thomas Booker IV, who plays 38% of snaps.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. worst short defense
keyMatchups.body: Lock's 0-9 yard throws have produced 0.386 EPA per attempt, and the Raiders allow the most EPA in the league on short passes. This is the matchup that should keep his efficiency up even if nothing big happens downfield.

keyMatchups.title: Smith-Njigba vs. a stingy WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas has held lead receivers 3.2 PPR points under their averages (7th) while getting torched by WR2s (32nd). If the Raiders shade coverage to Smith-Njigba, Lock's willingness to work Cooper Kupp and the tight end will decide the game. The Raiders already see an above-average share of targets go to tight ends.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders' rush vs. backup blockers
keyMatchups.body: The Raiders get hits on quarterbacks at the 8th-best rate, and Seattle is starting backups at guard and tackle. Lock's quick release is his best answer. Whether he can hold the ball for intermediate throws is the open question.

nextGame.watch: How often Lock is hit or rushed off his spot with Cross and Nelson out. If the pocket stays clean, the Raiders' short-pass weakness should hand him another efficient game.

restOfSeason.body:
Lock's runway looks like a couple more starts. Darnold's expected return of November 29 is an estimate, and once he is back Lock returns to QB2 with no fantasy relevance. In those starts, expect the volume to stay modest, because Seattle runs even though its run game is poor and its defense keeps games low-scoring. Expect the process to stay short and quick: roughly 180-230 passing yards and one or two touchdowns a game.

What is sustainable is the decision-making and the Smith-Njigba connection. What will regress is the zero interceptions, the near-2.0 EPA per deep attempt on five throws, and probably the bottom-of-the-league sack rate now that two starting linemen are out. He projects as a useful, efficient caretaker rather than the top-two passer his EPA rank suggests.
swingFactors: Timing of Darnold's return from the quad injury
Health of Cross and Nelson on the line
Whether the oblique limits his throwing

confidence.note: Three-game sample at odds with his career, an oblique strain, a likely short window before Darnold returns, and two linemen out.
